svg.title: Project Interview Coach example
svg.desc: A project interview question and a polished answer displayed in a macOS-style terminal window.

g.font-family: ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Monaco, Consolas, monospace
g.text: USER
How are relevant memories retrieved, and how does the system decide what to
include in the current turn?
PROJECT INTERVIEW COACH
We did not use embedding-based vector retrieval. Instead, we built a
lightweight, transparent, and auditable rule-based retrieval mechanism. It
has two stages: first, selecting candidate memories; and second, ranking them
by priority.
The first stage is candidate selection. When a user request arrives, the
system checks both the Episodic Memory from the current conversation and the
accumulated Durable Memory. It first removes memories that have expired or
have been superseded by newer facts.
It then checks whether each memory has a basic relationship with the current
request. A memory enters the candidate set only when its tags exactly match
the request tags, or when the request shares keywords with the memory content.
File-scoped memories are also checked against the files involved.
The second stage ranks candidates by scope fit, semantic relevance, and
recency. Specifically, the system considers:
1. Scope match: file, then session, then project.
2. Exact tag matches.
3. Memory type: constraint, decision, or error_resolution.
4. Keyword overlap between the request and memory content.
5. Recency when the other signals are similar.
Finally, the system selects at most the top three memories as Relevant Memory
and includes their types and scopes in the prompt. The model sees not only
what was remembered, but also what kind of information it is and where it
applies.
